items.stem: A running process requests data from a disk. To which state does it move?
options: Ready
Running
Terminated
Blocked
items.answer: Blocked
items.markingKey: Running → blocked while waiting for an I/O event; blocked → ready when the event completes.

items.stem: Explain why a process cannot move directly from the blocked state to the running state.
items.answer: When its I/O completes it must join the ready queue; only the scheduler can move a ready process to running, according to the scheduling algorithm.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Explain how an operating system maximises the use of the processor.
items.answer: Multitasking: while one process waits for I/O (blocked) another ready process is scheduled, so the CPU is rarely idle; interrupts let I/O run without the CPU waiting.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point, max 3 [3]

items.stem: The processes below are in the ready queue in the order shown, all arriving at time 0: P1: 3 ms; P2: 5 ms; P3: 7 ms. The operating system uses shortest job first (SJF, non-pre-emptive). Draw (write) the order in which the processes use the processor with start and end times, and calculate the average waiting time.
items.answer: P1 0–3 | P2 3–8 | P3 8–15; waiting times P1 = 0, P2 = 3, P3 = 8; average = 3.67 ms
items.markingKey: order/timeline correct (2); waiting time = completion − arrival − burst for each process (1); average 11 ÷ 3 = 3.67 ms (1) [4]

items.stem: The processes below are in the ready queue in the order shown, all arriving at time 0: P1: 10 ms; P2: 5 ms; P3: 2 ms; P4: 11 ms. The operating system uses shortest job first (SJF, non-pre-emptive). Draw (write) the order in which the processes use the processor with start and end times, and calculate the average waiting time.
items.markingKey: order/timeline correct (2); waiting time = completion − arrival − burst for each process (1); average 26 ÷ 4 = 6.5 ms (1) [4]

items.stem: The processes below are in the ready queue in the order shown, all arriving at time 0: P1: 3 ms; P2: 4 ms; P3: 11 ms; P4: 6 ms. The operating system uses round robin with a time quantum of 4 ms. Draw (write) the order in which the processes use the processor with start and end times, and calculate the average waiting time.
items.markingKey: order/timeline correct (2); waiting time = completion − arrival − burst for each process (1); average 31 ÷ 4 = 7.75 ms (1) [4]

items.stem: A multi-user server at City Central Library in Mexico City runs many processes at the same time. (a) Explain why round robin is suitable for an interactive multi-user system. (b) Describe two ways the operating system maximises the use of resources other than the processor.
items.answer: (a) Every user process gets the CPU regularly, so response times are short and no process is starved. (b) Memory management allocates/frees memory and uses virtual memory; spooling/buffering for printers; device drivers and I/O scheduling.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Diego is writing a report on how the operating system on a laptop shares the processor. (a) Describe the three main process states. (b) Describe two ways the operating system maximises the use of resources other than the processor.
items.answer: (a) Ready: waiting for the processor; running: being executed; blocked: waiting for an event such as I/O. (b) Memory management allocates/frees memory and uses virtual memory; spooling/buffering for printers; device drivers and I/O scheduling.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per state [3] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: A running process uses up its time slice. To which state does it move?
options: Suspended on disk
Ready
Terminated
Blocked
items.answer: Ready
items.markingKey: Running → ready when interrupted by the scheduler (time slice ends).

items.stem: A blocked process has its I/O operation completed. To which state does it move?
options: Blocked
Terminated
Ready
Running
items.answer: Ready
items.markingKey: Blocked → ready: it cannot go straight to running; it waits to be scheduled.

items.stem: Explain the difference between pre-emptive and non-pre-emptive scheduling.
items.answer: Pre-emptive: the OS can interrupt a running process (time slice/higher priority); non-pre-emptive: a process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Four jobs arrive together in the order P1: 3 ms; P2: 6 ms; P3: 5 ms; P4: 12 ms. Calculate the average waiting time using FCFS and using SJF, and state which algorithm gives the lower value.
items.answer: FCFS 6.5 ms; SJF 6.25 ms; SJF is lower
items.markingKey: FCFS average (1); SJF average (1); conclusion (1) [3]

items.stem: A process is in the running state. Which state does it move to when the time slice of the process ends?
options: Ready
Blocked
Running
Terminated
items.answer: Ready
items.markingKey: running → ready when the time slice of the process ends.

items.stem: A multi-user server at Northfield Academy in Cape Town runs many processes at the same time. Four processes arrive at time 0 with burst times P1 6 ms, P2 5 ms, P3 9 ms, P4 4 ms. Calculate the average waiting time using round robin with a 3 ms time slice.
items.markingKey: timeline (1); waiting times (1); average (1) [3]

items.stem: Freya is advising Harbour Bank on operating system configuration. Assess the choice of scheduling algorithm for Harbour Bank's server, comparing round robin, shortest job first and first come first served.
items.answer: Points in favour: RR gives fair, quick response for interactive users; SJF minimises average waiting time; FCFS simple with low overhead. Points against / limitations: RR has context-switch overhead and depends on quantum size; SJF needs burst times known and may starve long jobs; FCFS gives long waits behind long jobs (convoy effect). Conclusion: a pre-emptive algorithm such as RR (or multilevel feedback) suits mixed interactive workloads.
items.markingKey: Up to 4 marks for relevant technical points correctly applied to the scenario; up to 4 marks for developed explanation that weighs both sides and reaches a justified conclusion. Indicative content: RR gives fair, quick response for interactive users; SJF minimises average waiting time; FCFS simple with low overhead. / RR has context-switch overhead and depends on quantum size; SJF needs burst times known and may starve long jobs; FCFS gives long waits behind long jobs (convoy effect). [8]

items.answer: (a) P1 0–3 | P2 3–5 | P3 5–8 | P4 8–11 | P1 11–14 | P3 14–17 | P4 17–20 | P1 20–23 | P3 23–26 | P4 26–28 | P3 28–29; average waiting = 14 ms (b) Every user process gets the CPU regularly, so response times are short and no process is starved.
items.markingKey: (a) timeline [1]; waiting times [1]; average [1] [3] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: In paging, how is memory divided?
options: Into fixed-size blocks: pages in logical memory and page frames in physical memory
Into variable-size blocks based on program modules
Into sectors and tracks
Into one block per user
items.answer: Into fixed-size blocks: pages in logical memory and page frames in physical memory
items.markingKey: Pages are all the same size; segments vary.

items.stem: Explain the difference between paging and segmentation.
items.answer: Pages are fixed-size physical divisions; segments are variable-size logical divisions of the program (e.g. procedures); paging can cause internal fragmentation, segmentation external fragmentation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point, max 3 [3]

items.stem: Explain how virtual memory allows a program larger than RAM to run.
items.answer: Only the pages currently needed are loaded into RAM; others are kept on disk and swapped in when required (on a page fault).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: A system uses pages of 256 bytes. Calculate the page number and the offset of logical address 580.
items.answer: page 2, offset 68

items.stem: A process uses pages of 2048 bytes. Its page table is: page 0 → frame 10, page 1 → frame 18, page 2 → frame 6, page 3 → frame 3, page 4 → frame 15, page 5 → frame 5. Calculate the physical address of logical address 7446, showing your working.

The operating system of a computer at Atlas Museum uses paged virtual memory. (a) Pages are 512 bytes. Calculate the page number and offset for logical address 26595. (b) Explain the purpose of the page table.
items.answer: (a) page 51, offset 483 (b) Maps each page of the process to the frame in RAM holding it, with a flag to show whether the page is present.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Explain how disk thrashing can be reduced.
items.answer: Install more RAM; run fewer programs at once; use a better page replacement algorithm; reduce paging by increasing frame allocation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point, max 2 [2]

items.stem: Assertion (A): Virtual memory lets a computer run programs bigger than its RAM. Reason (R): Pages are of variable size. Which option is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
items.answer: A is true but R is false
items.markingKey: A is true; R is false: "Pages are of variable size." is incorrect.

items.stem: Nadia notices that a laptop with 4 GiB of RAM becomes very slow when many browser tabs are open. (a) Explain what is meant by virtual memory. (b) Suggest how the problem could be reduced.
items.answer: (a) Secondary storage used to extend RAM; pages swapped between RAM and disk as needed. (b) Add RAM; close programs; reduce number of processes; use an SSD for the swap area.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark per point, max 2 [2]

items.stem: A program of 10889 bytes is loaded into memory that uses pages of 1024 bytes. Calculate the number of pages needed and the internal fragmentation.
items.answer: 11 pages; 375 bytes unused

items.stem: The operating system of a computer at Riverside Medical Centre uses paged virtual memory. (a) Pages are 1024 bytes. Calculate the page number and offset for logical address 24873. (b) Explain the purpose of the page table.
items.answer: (a) page 24, offset 297 (b) Maps each page of the process to the frame in RAM holding it, with a flag to show whether the page is present.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Kwame is studying how a games console manages memory when several games are suspended. (a) Describe what happens when a page fault occurs. (b) Compare paging with segmentation.
items.answer: (a) Interrupt; OS finds the page on disk; chooses a frame (replacing a page using an algorithm, writing it back if changed); loads page; updates page table; process restarts. (b) Paging: fixed-size, physical division, internal fragmentation; segmentation: variable-size, logical division, external fragmentation.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per point, max 3 [3] (b) 1 mark per point, max 3 [3]

items.stem: Which stage of compilation removes white space and comments and converts the source code into tokens, adding identifiers to the symbol table?
options: Optimisation
Code generation
Lexical analysis
Syntax analysis
items.answer: Lexical analysis
items.markingKey: lexical analysis: removes white space and comments and converts the source code into tokens, adding identifiers to the symbol table.

items.stem: Explain why code optimisation is carried out.
items.answer: To make the object code run faster and/or use less memory, e.g. by removing redundant code or reusing results, without changing the program's result.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between the errors found in lexical analysis and syntax analysis.
items.answer: Lexical: invalid tokens/characters or identifiers (e.g. illegal symbol); syntax: tokens in an order that breaks grammar rules (e.g. missing bracket, IF without THEN).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem:

Speed ← 6 * 5 * Count
Write an optimised version and explain the optimisation made. (b) Explain why a compiled program runs faster than the same program run by an interpreter.
items.answer:
(a) Speed ← 30 * Count
The constant expression 6 * 5 is evaluated at compile time (30) (constant folding). (b) Translation happens once before execution; an interpreter translates each statement every time it is run.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark optimised code; 1 mark explanation [2] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: What is Backus–Naur form (BNF) used for?
options: Storing data in a database
Compressing source code
Converting infix to postfix
Describing the syntax rules of a language
items.answer: Describing the syntax rules of a language
items.markingKey: Meta-language with ::= and | to define grammar.

items.stem: Explain how a stack is used to evaluate an expression in Reverse Polish Notation.
items.answer: Read tokens left to right; push each operand; when an operator is read, pop the top two values, apply the operator (second popped op first popped) and push the result; the final value on the stack is the answer.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point, max 3 [3]

items.stem: Explain why a syntax diagram and a BNF definition can describe the same rule.
items.answer: Both are meta-languages defining the valid sequences of symbols; the diagram shows the alternatives and repetitions as paths/loops, BNF uses | and recursion.

Round robin
First come first served
Shortest job first
items.answer: Shortest job first

items.stem: The processes below are in the ready queue in the order shown, all arriving at time 0: P1: 11 ms; P2: 7 ms; P3: 8 ms. The operating system uses shortest job first (SJF, non-pre-emptive). Draw (write) the order in which the processes use the processor with start and end times, and calculate the average waiting time.
items.answer: P2 0–7 | P3 7–15 | P1 15–26; waiting times P1 = 15, P2 = 0, P3 = 7; average = 7.33 ms
items.markingKey: order/timeline correct (2); waiting time = completion − arrival − burst for each process (1); average 22 ÷ 3 = 7.33 ms (1) [4]

items.stem: Four jobs arrive together in the order P1: 8 ms; P2: 12 ms; P3: 6 ms; P4: 7 ms. Calculate the average waiting time using FCFS and using SJF, and state which algorithm gives the lower value.
items.answer: FCFS 13.5 ms; SJF 10 ms; SJF is lower
items.markingKey: FCFS average (1); SJF average (1); conclusion (1) [3]

items.stem: A multi-user server at Harbour Bank in Lagos runs many processes at the same time. (a) Explain how interrupts are used when a process requests data from a disk. (b) Four processes arrive at time 0 with burst times P1 8 ms, P2 3 ms, P3 10 ms, P4 4 ms. Calculate the average waiting time using round robin with a 3 ms time slice.
items.answer: (a) Process is blocked while disk transfers; disk controller sends an interrupt when done; ISR runs; process moves to ready. (b) P1 0–3 | P2 3–6 | P3 6–9 | P4 9–12 | P1 12–15 | P3 15–18 | P4 18–19 | P1 19–21 | P3 21–25; average waiting = 11.5 ms
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per point, max 3 [3] (b) timeline [1]; waiting times [1]; average [1] [3]

items.stem: What is virtual memory?
options: A type of ROM
Memory that is not used
Using part of secondary storage as if it were main memory
Memory inside the CPU
items.answer: Using part of secondary storage as if it were main memory
items.markingKey: Pages not in use are swapped out to disk; only needed pages are kept in RAM.

items.stem: Assertion (A): Disk thrashing slows a computer down. Reason (R): Segments must all be the same size. Which option is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
items.answer: A is true but R is false
items.markingKey: A is true; R is false: "Segments must all be the same size." is incorrect.

items.stem: A program of 47605 bytes is loaded into memory that uses pages of 4096 bytes. Calculate the number of pages needed and the internal fragmentation.
items.answer: 12 pages; 1547 bytes unused

items.stem: A program of 41122 bytes is loaded into memory that uses pages of 4096 bytes. Calculate the number of pages needed and the internal fragmentation.
items.answer: 11 pages; 3934 bytes unused

items.stem: Amara is studying how a games console manages memory when several games are suspended. (a) Pages are 512 bytes. Calculate the page number and offset for logical address 29457. (b) Describe what happens when a page fault occurs.
items.answer: (a) page 57, offset 273 (b) Interrupt; OS finds the page on disk; chooses a frame (replacing a page using an algorithm, writing it back if changed); loads page; updates page table; process restarts.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark per point, max 3 [3]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) What is held in the symbol table? (b) Which stage of compilation produces the object code (machine code) from the parse tree?
items.answer: (a) Identifiers with information such as their data type and memory location (b) Code generation
items.markingKey: (a) Built during lexical analysis and used in later stages. (b) code generation: produces the object code (machine code) from the parse tree.

items.stem: A compiler at Starlight Cinemas reports an error in the statement IF Total > 100 Discount ← 5 ENDIF. Explain the role of the symbol table in code generation.
items.answer: Gives the data type and memory address of each identifier so instructions can refer to the correct locations.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem:
A compiler optimises the code:
Width ← Rate + 6
Width ← Tax * 6
OUTPUT Width
Write an optimised version and explain the optimisation made.
items.answer:
Width ← Tax * 6
OUTPUT Width
The first value assigned to Width is never used before it is overwritten, so that statement is redundant.
items.markingKey: 1 mark optimised code; 1 mark explanation [2]

items.stem: During lexical analysis the statement Total ← Rate - Price + Width is processed. List the tokens produced and identify which tokens are entered into the symbol table.
items.answer: Tokens: Total, ←, Rate, -, Price, +, Width (7); symbol table: Total, Rate, Price, Width
items.markingKey: all 7 tokens (2); identifiers Total, Rate, Price, Width (1) [3]

items.stem:
Lakeside College uses a compiler to translate its stock control program into machine code. (a) Describe what happens during syntax analysis. (b) The compiler is given the code:
Index ← Total * Count + 5
Width ← Total * Count - Cost
Write an optimised version and explain the optimisation made. (c) Explain why a compiled program runs faster than the same program run by an interpreter.
items.answer:
(a) Tokens are parsed against the grammar (e.g. BNF); a parse tree is built; syntax errors are reported. (b) Temp ← Total * Count
Index ← Temp + 5
Width ← Temp - Cost
Total * Count is calculated twice (common subexpression), so it is calculated once and reused. (c) Translation happens once before execution; an interpreter translates each statement every time it is run.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per point, max 2 [2] (b) 1 mark optimised code; 1 mark explanation [2] (c) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Assertion (A): In RPN the operator comes before its operands. Reason (R): The most recent two operands are the ones needed by the next operator. Which option is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
items.answer: A is false but R is true
items.markingKey: A is false: "In RPN the operator comes before its operands." is incorrect; R is a true statement.

items.stem: Assertion (A): BNF can define identifiers of any length. Reason (R): A queue is used to evaluate RPN. Which option is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
items.answer: A is true but R is false
items.markingKey: A is true; R is false: "A queue is used to evaluate RPN." is incorrect.

items.stem: Evaluate the Reverse Polish Notation expression 5 10 9 * +. Show the contents of the stack after each operator is processed.
items.markingKey: stack after each operator: [5, 90]; (95) (2); final value 95 (1) [3]

items.stem: A compiler being developed at Palm Grove Hotel in Lisbon converts expressions to Reverse Polish Notation. (a) Convert E - (Y - E * E) to Reverse Polish Notation. (b) Explain why RPN is used by the interpreter.
items.answer: (a) E Y E E * - - (b) No brackets or precedence rules needed; evaluated left to right in one pass using a stack.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark operands; 1 mark operators [2] (b) 1 mark each [2]
